messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 44
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nurse
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Mirror Checking: keep checking mirrors, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

It has been six months since An’s life fractured. The break happened on a Tuesday night in the third-level of the hospital parking garage. Walking to his car after a grueling twelve-hour shift, he was preoccupied with thoughts of the dinner his wife, Lena, had waiting for him. He didn't hear them until they had him pinned against the cold concrete pillar. The memory doesn’t play like a film; it surfaces in a series of stark, silent photographs that ambush his waking thoughts. There is the image of the chipped linoleum knife, held inches from his face. There is the image of the second man’s worn-out sneakers, planted a foot from his own. And there is the image of his own terrified eyes reflected back at him in the side mirror of a parked sedan. They took his wallet and phone, and just as he thought it was over, a boot slammed into his ribs, sending a shock of white-hot agony through his side.

In the weeks that followed, the pain in his side faded, but a phantom version of it remained. Whenever one of the photographic stills of the attack would flash into his mind—in the middle of dispensing medication, during a conversation with Lena—the ghost of that kick would bloom in his ribs, sharp and sudden enough to make him catch his breath. Sleep became a nightly battle he always lost. The moment his head hit the pillow, his mind would switch on, a frantic sentinel scanning the darkness of the room for threats. He would lie awake for hours, convinced every creak of the house was an intruder, finally succumbing to an exhausted, dream-plagued sleep just hours before his alarm was due to go off.

His world began to shrink, reconfigured around the central principle of safety. At work, he would no longer eat in the main cafeteria, instead taking his lunch in the small breakroom on his ward where he could sit in a specific chair in the corner, his back to the wall, the door in his full line of sight. Walking the long hospital corridors, his head was on a constant swivel, his gaze flicking to every doorway, every intersection, and he developed a nervous habit of glancing over his shoulder every twenty paces to ensure no one was following too closely. The walk to his car became a meticulously planned ordeal, a route he would mentally rehearse before leaving the ward.

At home, silence became the enemy. An filled every moment with noise to keep the images at bay. He listened to podcasts while showering, kept the television on from the moment he walked in until he went to bed, and took on extra shifts just to keep his mind occupied. He knew Lena was worried. He saw it in the way she watched him, the way she would try to start conversations about their future, only for him to deflect with a vague answer. He couldn’t explain to her that he no longer believed he had one. It felt to him as though all the good in his life had been used up before that night, and now there was nothing left ahead.

A deeper, more insidious belief took root: that there was something about him that had invited the attack. He would spend long minutes in front of the bathroom mirror, not grooming, but searching his own face for the flaw, the weakness, the mark of a victim he was sure the men had seen. He was certain he had been chosen for a reason, that he was intrinsically broken in some way. This conviction settled over him like a shroud, and the man he was before—a confident nurse, a loving husband—seemed like a stranger from a different life. He finally made the call to seek help after Lena found him standing frozen in the hallway, staring at his own reflection in the darkened living room window, his hand pressed to his side. He came to therapy not with any real hope, but with the quiet, desperate fear that this hyper-alert, haunted version of himself was all he would ever be again.
